scenes.contextualRelevance: Description of the feelings and atmosphere during Aldrich's audition and interaction with Gene Simmons.

narrativeProgression.description: The musician reminisces about how he felt when he auditioned for Kiss.
The musician says that he felt like it might be his destiny to join Kiss, even though he hadn't planned on it.
The musician laughs and says that he was scared to look the band members in the eyes because they weren't wearing their makeup.
The musician adds that he felt like he would be breaking the rules if he looked at the band members in the face.
The musician says that, in the end, he was too young to join the band at that time.
The musician says that he had some good jam sessions with the band and got to play through big Marshall stacks for the first time.
The musician notes that he had always played through a half stack before.
The unseen person asks the musician why he didn't get the gig.
The musician says that he was too young and the band knew it.
The musician goes on to explain that being in a band is like being in a family, and everyone needs to be comfortable with each other.
The musician says that the band would have been on a bus and in hotels together, and that it needed to be comfortable for everyone.
The musician adds that the band probably could see that he wasn't comfortable because he was so young and nervous.
The musician finishes his explanation by saying that the band wasn't going to be comfortable on a tour bus with a kid.
The unseen person asks the musician what it was like being with Gene Simmons.
The unseen person notes that Gene Simmons sometimes seems like a very demanding person, both as a musician and a businessman.
The musician recalls that Gene Simmons was funny and kind.
The musician says that Gene Simmons spent the most time with him in the studio while Kiss was working on the 'Creatures of the Night' album.
The musician remembers that there was a song called 'War Machine' that Simmons asked him to play on to see how he would record it.
The musician thought the riff was really cool but different, and he had never heard anything like it before.
The musician recalls that Simmons asked him if he ever played major scales, and he had to admit he didn't know what a major scale was.

The musician says that Gene Simmons wrote down three songs on a napkin for him to learn.
The musician learned the songs and went to rehearsal with the band.
The musician was invited back for a second audition.
One of the songs the band wanted him to learn for the second audition was 'Black Diamond', which the musician says was Kiss' version of 'Stairway to Heaven'.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Back in the day in 1982 you auditioned for Kiss, you were basically 18 years old at the time
or something.
What was it like?
You're standing there with the biggest rock bands on the planet and you're just basically
a kid.
What did it feel like at that point?
Well, it was kind of, I felt like it was just kind of, you know, when you think about
Hollywood, you think about people come from all over the world and they come to Hollywood
to make it.
And I didn't plan on it being with Kiss, but I felt like, okay, this might be what I'm
supposed to do, you know, to come to Hollywood and join Kiss, you know.
I just didn't really think about it too much.
I was definitely scared to look at them in the eyes in a sense because at that time people
had never seen them without their makeup and I felt like I was breaking the rules, you
know, if I looked them in their face.
But, but I mean, in the end I was just too young, you know, I think, but we had, we had
some good jams and it was the first time I ever got to play through giant stacks of marshals,
you know, I had never done that before.
It always been like a half stack.
Yeah.
But, you know, why, how did you, how did that then, you know, why didn't you get the gig
at that point?
I just, I was too young.
They knew it, you know, I mean, I was, I was a kid.
These guys were, you know, international rock stars and I was just a kid.
I think, you know, my experience, look, here's the thing, David, is, is you want to get
a gig?
It doesn't, it's 50% how good you are and it's 50% how cool you can hang out together.
Yeah.
Because you, in a band, you got to be like, it's like a family.
It's like you got to be able to hang out together and, and be comfortable and not have any
kind of weird, anything, anything weird going on because, you know, you're going to be together
on a bus, you're going to be together in hotels.
It needs to be comfortable for the band and probably they could see that I was not comfortable
because I was so young, I was nervous.
And, and so they would, you know, that's probably why they decided this is, my plan was probably
okay, but they're not going to be comfortable on a tour bus with a kid.
What was like, you know, being with Jean Simons, you know, he does sometimes seem like a
very demanding, not only a musician, but a businessman in a way, you know, what was he
like?
He was very, he was very funny, you know, he was very kind and, and he basically spent
the most time with me in the studio when they were working on the record creatures
of the night at that time.
Yeah.
And now, I remember there was a song called War Machine, I think, and I played, he asked
me to play guitar on the song, just check how I would record, what I would do on the recording.
And I remember playing that song thinking, this is a crazy riff, it's really cool, but
it's very different.
And I never heard a riff like that before.
I was trying to figure out what kid it is, you know.
Yeah.
And then I was playing some other stuff and Jean said to me, hey, Doug, do you ever play
major scales?
And I said, major scales, which I didn't even know what a major scale was.
And he goes, you know, do rei mi fa, so I go, oh, of course I know what that is.
It's like Michael Shanker plays that stuff all the time, you know.
And I started playing, he goes, yeah, that's great, that's great.
So then they invited me to come to play live with them.
And Jean wrote down three songs on a napkin or a piece of paper I should say.
I learned the songs and I went to the rehearsal and we practiced them.
And then they called me back to the second time.
And they asked me to learn, well, one of the songs that they wanted me to learn on the
first time was Black Diamond because that's kind of what's kind of like their version of
that was kind of like their version of stairway to heaven.
Yeah.
That was like their stairway to heaven.
And so we played that.
But then when I came back, they wanted me to learn the Fritbrox city.
That was really cool.
And yeah, I just think that the second audition I started to get really like, wow, this
might be happening.
And it was very strange for me.
Yeah.
Is that I also somewhere read the story that you, the Jean Simons gave you a phone number
and that you called him.
Is that story true?
Yes, it's true.
He wrote down his number on the very first day.
Oh, yeah.
And then he, you know, I called him whenever I'm tour and he hung up on me.
Yeah.
It must have felt weird at the time when you were young and everything and they were like
big rock stars.
But you know, you know, well, yeah, I felt it was weird by, you know, it's all fun.
It's funny now.
It's a part of my history.
So I don't really, I'm glad it happened like that.
Thanks for watching.
And if you want more music news, just subscribe to Old MgdrTV and press that little bell
to get notifications.
